- rows: 201
- sha256: `83C62D610F0824AF059AF9F66E1B9A0C08A50C1866658805EB6B7315D463216B`

Headline yearly numbers for `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40`:

| year | PnL | Sharpe | max DD inside year | avgGross | maxGross |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2018 | `-$2.029k` | -0.52 | `-$6.785k` | 0.532x | 0.647x |
| 2022 | `-$2.617k` | -0.12 | `-$15.439k` | 0.614x | 0.655x |

2018 diagnosis:

- 2018 is a partial-book year: the engine starts on 2018-04-30 and has only broad/local sleeves.
  YDAY and intraday WFO do not contribute in 2018.
- The full-year loss is concentrated in two market selloff months:

| month | portfolio PnL | SPY 09:30->15:55 month return | avgGross |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2018-10 | `-$3.170k` | -6.85% | 0.596x |
| 2018-12 | `-$2.393k` | -9.30% | 0.628x |

The rest of the partial year is net positive. Closed-trade attribution by sleeve is mildly negative
on both sleeves: broad `-$0.614k`, local `-$0.934k`. Worst closed-trade tickers are GE `-$0.641k`,
NVDA `-$0.520k`, EBAY `-$0.404k`, MU `-$0.325k`, and AMAT `-$0.282k`.

Read: 2018 is not a single broken sleeve. It is a young partial book with positive market beta
getting hit by the Q4 2018 selloff before enough good months accumulate.

2022 diagnosis:

- 2022 is different: all three lead sleeves are active.
- Broad/local lose in the bear regime, while YDAY offsets most of it:

| sleeve | closed trades | PnL | mean trade | win rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `broad_adv10_g2_dd85` | 2,294 | `-$3.568k` | `-$1.56` | 45.8% |
| `local_xs_full_s10` | 2,500 | `-$4.173k` | `-$1.67` | 46.2% |
| `yday_ex6_actual` | 65 | `$7.656k` | `$117.78` | 50.8% |

The worst 2022 equity months are all broad market drawdown months:

| month | portfolio PnL | SPY 09:30->15:55 month return | avgGross |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2022-09 | `-$7.293k` | -9.60% | 0.615x |
| 2022-04 | `-$6.967k` | -8.77% | 0.593x |
| 2022-12 | `-$6.862k` | -6.14% | 0.627x |
| 2022-06 | `-$6.778k` | -8.63% | 0.614x |

Worst 2022 closed-trade tickers: MU `-$3.316k`, META `-$2.701k`, NFLX `-$1.978k`, PYPL
`-$1.803k`, ADBE `-$1.483k`, INTU `-$1.270k`, ORCL `-$1.069k`, MMM `-$1.049k`, AMD
`-$0.884k`, SBUX `-$0.853k`.

Daily SPY relationship:

| year | daily corr(portfolio PnL, SPY intraday return) | beta dollars | PnL on SPY-down days | PnL on SPY-up days |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2018 | 0.782 | `$32.9k` | `-$16.740k` | `$14.712k` |
| 2022 | 0.812 | `$86.2k` | `-$110.915k` | `$108.298k` |

Read: the lead book is not market neutral. It is a long-biased mean-reversion/loser-rebound book.
That is why 2022 nearly washes out: down days are very expensive, and up days almost offset them
but not quite. YDAY is the only sleeve that clearly helps in 2022.

Implication:

- The two negative years do not point to a reconstruction bug.
- 2018 is mostly sample-start/partial-book plus Q4 selloff.
- 2022 is a genuine regime weakness: broad/local hold-20 loser rebound struggles in persistent
  bear-market legs.
- Next useful research is a causal market-regime overlay or beta throttle, tested without using
  future returns. The overlay should target broad/local exposure during persistent SPY downtrend
  regimes while preserving YDAY, because YDAY is the 2022 offset rather than the problem.

### 6.95 Independent audit of 6.93 Polygon-62 no-intraday robustness stress

Run 2026-09-11, 10:11-10:25 ET (machine clock Calgary 08:11-08:25 MDT). Commit `de2cf77`.
Numbered 6.95 because a parallel session appended 6.94 while this audit was running; 6.94 is
outside this audit's scope and I did not review it.

Contract kept: read and re-measure only. No code changed, nothing committed, no off-limits folder
opened (including `scratch/**`), sealed 2025-2026 untouched, nothing deleted. Every re-run in this
audit wrote to the scratchpad only; I redirected the stress script's output paths in-process
before calling it. Across every `STOCKS_POLYGON*` file and both Polygon scripts, hashed at the start
and at the end, the only difference is the two 6.94 files the parallel session created.

#### Verdicts

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| 6.93 implementation | **PASS** — every output reproduces, most of them byte for byte |
| 6.93 reporting | **WARN** — three readings overstate what the numbers show; the corrections favour B |
| Headline A/B no-intraday stats | **Match** to the cent |
| "B lead, A higher-gross reference, `intraday_ex10` FAIL" | **Supported** — and the A-versus-B gap is larger than 6.93 shows |
| Anything forcing a downgrade to FAIL | **No** |
| Verdict for `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40` | **WARN.** "Stronger than before" holds for cost, gross and bootstrap tail. It does not hold for concentration |
| More audit of 6.93 before the survivorship work | **Not needed.** Carry the text corrections below; the survivorship-aware universe is now the blocker that matters most |

#### 1. Data path: Polygon-62 2018-2024 only

- **Pipeline only.** The stress script reads the 6.92 pipeline's daily features and 09:35 cache
  (lines 79-87), rebuilds signals with the pipeline's own `load_signals`, and simulates through the
  pipeline's `simulate`. That function sets the shared engine's window to 2018-01-01 → 2024-12-31
  and passes Polygon-derived prices.
- **Every file it reads is code-backed.** The four sleeve ledgers and the one-engine equity and
  trade files are all written by the pipeline's `main()`. No hand-made or orphan artifact is read.
- **No ML.** No learning library or model references in either script.
- **Databento: imported but never loaded.** The pipeline imports the broad-overlay module for its
  simulator and config, then feeds it a panel built from Polygon daily features for the 62 names.
  The Databento parquet loader is never called.
- **No off-limits path references** in either script.
- **No sealed data.** The bars pickle holds 63 symbols and 8,728,437 bars, 2018-01-02 09:30 to
  2024-12-31 16:00. The feature caches end 2024-12-31. The engine window is 2018-04-30 → 2024-12-31.

**One provenance correction for 6.91 and 6.92.** Both record the bars pickle as `C9E1FF1D…`. The
file on disk is `5359E4B3D31B981AFBF378DB16F9DFB1B05A2495ACD7C94A41ECBD580218CA44`, written at
05:37:51 local, twenty minutes before the features were built at 05:58:01. The recorded hash is
not a hash of this file — most likely it came from an earlier bridge run. What matters is proven
independently: I rebuilt the daily features from the pickle on disk with the builder's own
function. The result is **byte-identical** to the cache 6.92 hashed (`FAFA37EC…`), and the frames
are equal. The data path is intact; only the recorded hash needs updating.

A timing question I also closed: the `NO_INTRADAY` one-engine files were written at 05:54:42,
thirteen seconds before the pipeline script's last edit, and the current pipeline no longer writes
them. They are orphans, but the stress script does not read them, and their summary rows equal the
current `NO_ML` summary rows for both no-intraday portfolios to the cent.

#### 2. Cap and cost sweep

- **Grid complete:** 160 rows, 160 unique keys, zero duplicates, zero missing, zero extra
  (2 portfolios × 4 ticker caps × 5 gross caps × 4 costs). Every row's `portfolio` name agrees
  with its key columns.
- **Resume is safe by construction.** Completed keys are skipped (lines 100-116), each new cell is
  appended once, and the file is rewritten after every cell. Nothing can be counted twice.
- **Resume is safe in fact.** I re-simulated six cells with the current code:

| Cell | Why this cell | CSV P&L | My P&L |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| A, ticker 20%, gross 1.0, 4 bps | written by the timed-out first process | `$95,233.13` | identical |
| A, ticker 20%, gross 1.0, 9 bps | written by the timed-out first process | `$81,425.47` | identical |
| A, ticker 40%, gross 2.0, 4 bps | A baseline | `$135,816.68` | identical |
| B, ticker 40%, gross 1.75, 4 bps | B baseline | `$109,480.37` | identical |
| B, ticker 40%, gross 1.0, 4 bps | quoted in 6.93 | `$107,777.31` | identical |
| B, ticker 40%, gross 1.75, 24 bps | quoted in 6.93 | `$47,768.91` | identical |

  Drawdown, Sharpe and max gross agree too; the largest difference is `1.5e-11`.
- **Cost reaches the engine.** The engine reads `COST_BPS` at call time (line 251). Measured on the
  re-simulated trades, the entry cost is exactly 4.00 bps of notional at base and exactly 24.00 bps
  in the 24-bps cell. The cost is charged on both entry and exit, so "4 bps" means 4 bps per side.
- **Both caps act before orders.** In the engine, each day's target is first scaled per ticker
  (lines 315-331) and then scaled to the remaining gross capacity (lines 334-337). Only then are
  orders filled (lines 339-382), and nothing is re-scaled after P&L.
- **Every sweep number quoted in 6.93 matches the CSV:** all eight ticker-cap rows, all eight
  cost rows, and the gross-1.0 figure. No cell of the 160 loses money. The worst is B at ticker
  20%, gross 1.0, 24 bps: `$41,348`, Sharpe 0.69.

**What "ticker cap" actually limits.** The cap applies to each day's new orders in a ticker, not
to total exposure in it. A twenty-day sleeve adds a layer every day, and yday can enter a name
that broad or local already hold. Measured on entry notional:

- **A** holds more than 40% of equity in one name at some point for 42 tickers, peaking at 44.8%
  (ORCL, 2022-02-18).
- **B** peaks at 39.3%, so it never breaches.

This is also why the 20% and 30% cap rows move so much: they mostly shrink the one-name yday
position, which is 35-40% of equity per trade.

#### 3. Leverage and cash: true at the close, not during the day

The sanity file is correct as written. B's max gross is 0.677x, A's 0.773x, and neither ever
ends a day with negative cash. But both figures are taken at the **close**, after the same-day
yday position has exited at 15:55. The engine's own sequence — entries at the open or 09:35,
exits at 15:55 or the close — matches the real day, and between those two moments the book is
bigger.

I measured this three independent ways, and they agree:

| | B no-intraday | A no-intraday | B all-sleeve |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Max gross at the close (6.93) | 0.677x | 0.773x | 0.760x |
| **Max gross just after the day's entries** | **≈1.06x** | **≈1.21x** | ≈1.45x |
| Days above 1.0x | 85 | 196 | 438 |
| **Cash just after the day's entries: worst** | **−$5.3k (−5.3% of equity)** | **−$29.5k (−15.9%)** | −$42.1k (−33.5%) |
| Days with negative cash after entries | 85 (5.1%) | 196 (11.8%) | 439 (26.4%) |

For the two no-intraday books the day counts from the gross route and the cash route match
exactly, as they must for a long-only book; the all-sleeve book differs by one day because its
intraday sleeve also sells short (1,408 short trades).

The third route is the sweep itself. A 1.0x gross cap cannot bind a book whose
gross never exceeds 0.773x, yet it cuts A from `$135.8k` to `$109.6k` and B from `$109.5k` to
`$107.8k`. In the base runs the 1.75x and 2.0x caps never bind (`gross_scale` below 1 on zero days).

What this means:

- No position is financed overnight, so the economics are unaffected.
- The book needs a **margin account**: B borrows up to about 5% of equity intraday, A up to 16%.
- 6.93's sentence "the lead is not relying on high portfolio leverage" is right for B — peak
  about 1.06x, and a 1.0x cap costs `$1.7k`. It is not right for A, whose P&L falls 19% under a
  1.0x cap.
- `tickerCapAppliedBeforeOrders` and `grossCapAppliedBeforeOrders` in the sanity file are
  hard-coded `True` (lines 262-263), not measured. They happen to be true, as section 2 shows,
  but a check that cannot be false is not a check.

#### 4. Concentration

**Base rows match exactly.** The concentration file's base P&L, drawdown and Sharpe equal the
one-engine output. Its top-ticker share, top-ten share and effective ticker count equal my own
computation from trade P&L to four decimals. Closed-trade P&L sums exactly to equity P&L for all
four portfolios (no trade is open at the end), so the shares use the right denominator.

**Two readings need correcting.**

- **The four-sleeve book's low effective ticker count comes from its losers, not its winners.**
  `effectiveTickers` is `total² / Σ pnl²` over signed ticker P&L. The four-sleeve book has 26
  losing tickers worth −$39.4k, which shrinks the total and inflates the ratio. Counting winners
  only, the four-sleeve B is at 11.8 effective tickers and the three-sleeve B at 11.0.
- **Both books depend on the same winners, by the same dollars.** The top ten tickers earn
  `$78.5k` in the three-sleeve B and `$77.6k` in the four-sleeve B, with seven names in common.
  TSLA alone is `$29.3k` against `$26.9k`. The entire difference is in the other 52 names:
  +`$31.0k` against −`$0.7k`. That gap is essentially the intraday sleeve's −`$20.9k`. So removing
  intraday removes a losing sleeve. It does not make the book less dependent on its winners — 72%
  of the lead's P&L still comes from 10 of 62 names.

**The no-refill drop tests are described correctly — they are not presented as refill
counterfactuals.** But "deliberately punitive" is probably too generous to the book. This document
already measured the realistic version on the 2023-2024 clean book, in the corrected refill test
(6.60 series): refilling with runner-ups recovered **3.3%** of the removed P&L, and landed almost on
top of the no-refill number. An independent ML-sleeve re-run gave +1.5%. If that carries over to
2018-2024 — not yet measured — then B dropping its top ten names, `$31.0k` against `$109.5k`, is
close to realistic rather than a harsh lower bound. The drop rows also subtract each trade's whole
P&L on its exit date, so their totals are exact but their drawdowns are approximate.

#### 5. Bootstrap

- **Right series.** Each portfolio's own daily equity P&L, 1,663 days and 81 months.
- **Fixed seed.** `default_rng(20260911)`, with one generator drawn in a fixed order.
- **Byte-identical rerun.** Re-running the script's function reproduces the file byte for byte
  (`777AF543…`, as 6.93 records).
- **Independent reimplementation matches.** My own NumPy version — same seed and draw order, my
  own drawdown code — gives every quantile, drawdown quantile and loss probability with **zero**
  difference. The p01, p05, median, drawdown p50, drawdown p95 and Pr(P&L ≤ 0) are all computed as
  labelled.
- **The claim holds.** No-intraday p01 is positive in both modes: B `$29.2k` day, `$36.9k` month
  block. The four-sleeve book's day-bootstrap p01 is negative: B −`$4.1k`; A −`$4.6k`, a row 6.93
  did not quote. Its month-block p01 is positive, as 6.93 says.
- **The sign is robust to the seed, but the all-sleeve number is barely below zero.** Across five
  other seeds, B no-intraday day p01 stays between `$26.6k` and `$32.1k`, and B all-sleeve between
  −`$0.9k` and −`$4.1k`. So the robust contrast is the size of the gap — about `$30k` against
  about zero — rather than the sign of a number close to zero.
- **What the bootstrap is not.** Pr(P&L ≤ 0) of 0.02% is one draw in 5,000, the resolution floor. A
  day bootstrap also breaks the multi-day holding structure, so it understates drawdown clustering;
  the month-block rows are the better guide to the tail. And neither bootstrap samples which
  tickers win, so neither says anything about the concentration in section 4.

#### 6. 2022 diagnostics

Every figure quoted in 6.93 matches the CSV and my own recomputation:

- 2022 for B: −`$2.617k`.
- By sleeve: broad −`$3.568k`, local −`$4.173k`, yday +`$7.656k`.
- Worst months: 2022-09 −`$7.293k`, 2022-04 −`$6.967k`, 2022-12 −`$6.862k`, 2022-06 −`$6.778k`.
- Worst tickers: MU −`$3.316k`, META −`$2.701k`, NFLX −`$1.978k`, PYPL −`$1.803k`, ADBE −`$1.483k`.

**But the sleeve split is on a different basis from the year it sits next to.** The sleeve figures
are closed-trade P&L by exit date, and they sum to **−`$0.086k`**. The yearly −`$2.617k` is
mark-to-market. The `$2.53k` gap is positions straddling the year ends: 356 trades entered in 2021
and exited in 2022, and 368 entered in 2022 and exited in 2023. For A the sleeves sum to −`$0.483k`
against −`$3.666k`. A reader will take "broad −3.6, local −4.2, yday +7.7" as the anatomy of a
−`$2.6k` year, and it is not.

#### 7. Side effects and git

- **Writes.** The stress script writes exactly its six new files and nothing else (lines 134, 138,
  186, 241, 268, 319-320).
- **No overwrites.** All 6.91 and 6.92 outputs predate the 6.93 run (06:04 or earlier, against
  08:00), and all were unchanged throughout this audit.
- **Nothing deleted.** 21 cache pickles (17 before plus the four Polygon pickles) and 10 research
  parquet files present.
- **Git status.** The tracked modified files are `SCRATCHPAD.md`, `TASK.md` and
  `monitor/paper_pnl_compare.json` — owner notes and a parallel futures session, none related to
  6.93. `raits/research/` is untracked as a whole. The `STOCKS_POLYGON62_*` CSVs do not appear in
  git status at all because CSVs are ignored. So git cannot tell Codex's files from anyone else's
  here; the evidence of ownership is modification time, and that is consistent with 6.93's claims.

#### Minimal fixes

1. **Sanity** (`stocks_polygon62_no_intraday_robustness.py:245-269`). Add post-entry gross and
   post-entry cash, derived from the trades as in section 3, or better recorded by the engine after

None of these changes a number in 6.93.

#### Answering the remaining questions

**Is "B lead, A higher-gross reference, `intraday_ex10` FAIL" supported?** Yes, on all three.

- **`intraday_ex10`:** the sleeve loses `$20.9k` inside B all-sleeve, and removing it improves P&L,
  drawdown, Sharpe and the bootstrap tail.
- **B over A:** A earns more (`$135.8k` against `$109.5k`) at the same Sharpe (1.251 against 1.256).
  But it needs up to 16% intraday margin on 12% of days, peaks near 1.2x gross, loses 19% under a
  1.0x cap, and exceeds its own nominal 40% ticker cap in held exposure. B stays below every one of
  those lines, so the case for B as lead is stronger than 6.93 makes it.

**Is more audit needed before moving on?** Not of this step. The computation is sound and
reproducible. The survivorship-aware universe is the right next blocker, and this audit adds a
reason to hurry: 72% of the lead's P&L comes from ten names that are, by construction, survivors —
TSLA, NVDA, NOW, PANW, AMAT and five more. That is exactly the shape survivorship bias inflates. The
concentration WARN and the survivorship blocker are therefore the same question, and the
survivorship test is the one that can answer it.

Blockers before a production PASS:

- survivor universe, not survivorship-aware;
- 2023-2024 already opened in earlier research;
- 2018-2019 are partial-book years;
- concentration: ten names carry 72%, with refill evidence suggesting that is close to real;
- intraday margin to be confirmed as available on the live account type.

- same-winner dependence, `$78.5k` against `$77.6k`;

### 6.99 Independent audit of the local hold-5 high-vol challenger (6.96-6.98)

Run 2026-09-11, 12:32-12:50 ET (machine clock Calgary 10:32-10:50 MDT). Commit `de2cf77`.

Contract kept: read and re-measure only. No code changed, nothing committed, no off-limits folder
opened, sealed 2025-2026 untouched, nothing deleted. Every re-run wrote to the scratchpad; for the
byte-for-byte reproduction I redirected the canonical runner's four output paths in-process before
calling it. Across every `STOCKS_POLYGON*` file, the Polygon scripts, the engine and the Polygon
pickles, hashed at the start and at the end, nothing changed.

#### Verdicts

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Implementation | **PASS** — does exactly what 6.98 says; all four outputs reproduce byte for byte |
| Causality of the SPY trigger | **PASS** — shifted one session, threshold exactly `>= 0.020`, reproduced independently |
| Research design | **WARN** — rule, threshold and action were chosen as the best of 96 configurations on the same 2018-2024 data, 2022 included |
| Stated mechanism ("the exit horizon beats throttling") | **Not supported** — at unchanged notional the shorter exit **loses** money; the gain comes from the 4× notional |
| Replace `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40` as lead? | **No.** Keep base as lead. Keep this as an exploratory challenger, relabelled as what it is: a regime size-up of local, braked by a 5-day exit |
| Is the P&L gain caused by higher local notional? | **Yes, entirely.** And about half of it is compounding |

#### 1. Implementation

**Hashes.** The runner is `784bd273fe405d673eb579a42ec81d701d76d066`, as 6.98 states. The four
outputs reproduce **byte for byte**: summary `3E98C4EA…` and yearly `B217AFD3…` (both as recorded
in 6.98), equity `E8D8834D…`, trades `49826AA2…`.

**Every expected figure matches to the cent:**

| Portfolio | P&L | CAGR | DD | Sharpe | avg / max gross |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A candidate | `$145,391.23` | 22.66% | `−$18,559.24` | 1.2767 | 0.694x / 0.930x |
| B candidate | `$116,977.08` | 19.81% | `−$15,889.03` | 1.2800 | 0.608x / 0.811x |

- **Yearly figures match the brief:**
  - A: −2,335 · 12,795 · 29,095 · 26,832 · −313 · 39,131 · 40,186.
  - B: −2,029 · 11,138 · 24,730 · 21,702 · +94 · 30,759 · 30,583.
- **B equals the 6.97 probe exactly** on P&L, drawdown, Sharpe, average gross and max gross.
- **Base runs reproduce.** Through the same inputs, base A and B reproduce `$135,816.68` and
  `$109,480.37`.

**Only the local exits change.** I diffed the base and candidate signal frames column by column:

- **Rows:** 31,193 in both. Only `hold_days` and `exit_date` differ, on exactly **550 rows**.
- **Which rows:** all `local_xs_full_s10` — 55 dates × 10 names; 410 in 2020, 140 in 2022.
- **Other sleeves:** no broad or yday row changes.
- **Other columns:** entry price, side, `raw_strength`, `strength`, entry and exit style, ticker and
  date are identical on every row. Trade count is unchanged at 31,193.

**Right inputs, right path.**

- **Inputs:** the Polygon-62 feature caches and sleeve ledgers, through the 6.92 pipeline's
  `load_signals`. Signals are filtered to the three no-intraday sleeves before anything else, so
  `intraday_ex10` cannot enter.
- **Simulation:** runs through `poly.simulate` → `engine.simulate`. This is a full engine replay,
  not a post-hoc scaling.
- **Clean:** no ML, no Databento, no off-limits references and no delete calls in any of the four
  scripts. Each writes only its own outputs. The bars pickle ends 2024-12-31.

**One engine note.** The engine's hash is `814ed30213dfcf2ae30c298cafccb3e97578c2d7`, not the
`d8d73153…` recorded in 6.88. It was edited on 2026-09-10 at 21:09 local, before every Polygon run.
Line 161 now reads the regenerated local ledger, which is fix 3 from 6.88. That function is not on
the Polygon path.

#### 2. Causality of the SPY trigger

`spy_regimes()` in the overlay script (lines 27-68):

- takes SPY's 15:55 close from the Polygon bars pickle;
- computes close-to-close returns;
- takes the 20-session standard deviation and **shifts it one session** (line 42);
- sets the flag at `spy_prev_vol20 >= 0.020` (line 51).

On entry day *d*, the flag therefore uses returns through *d−1* only. Entries are at the open or
09:35 and exits later, so nothing from day *d* or after can reach it.

I rebuilt the volatility independently from the pickle and it reproduces the script's flag on every
date. Two small notes:

- Sessions without both a 09:30 and a 15:55 bar are dropped by an inner merge, so a return can
  occasionally span two sessions.
- Dates with no flag default to off.

Neither creates leakage. **Causality: PASS.**

What is not causal in the ordinary sense is the **choice** of the rule. The 2.0% threshold came
from the 6.96 sweep (36 configurations), and the hold-5, local-only action from the 6.97 sweep (60
configurations). Both sweeps were scored on the same 2018-2024 sample, with 2022 as the explicit
target. The candidate is rank 1 of 60, and only 8 of the 60 beat base.

#### 3. Exit-date replacement

- **Only when triggered.** Hold 20 → 5 happens only on flagged local rows, and all 550 local rows
  on trigger dates had a valid 5th exit, so none fell back to hold 20.
- **Same convention as hold 20.** The 5th exit is computed per ticker by row count (four rows
  ahead) — the inclusive convention the pipeline already uses for the 20th exit (nineteen rows
  ahead).
- **One wrinkle.** Row count is not session count when a ticker has a day missing from the filtered
  feature table. On the SPY calendar:
  - **490 of 550** switched trades exit on the true 5th session;
  - **58** exit on the 6th, 1 on the 7th and 1 on the 8th.

  The base's hold-20 exits have the same property. Minor, and pre-existing.

#### 4. Sizing: disclosed, but not measured

The engine sizes each sleeve's day as `equity_open × weight / hold` (lines 310-312), so hold 5
quadruples the per-entry local notional on trigger days. 6.98 says so. What it does not show is
what that does to the book:

| Local sleeve, B | Base | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| New local notional, 2020 episode window | `$88k` | `$214k` |
| New local notional, 2022 episode window | `$71k` | `$148k` |
| Local exposure during the 2020 episode, average | 0.349x | **0.424x** |
| Local exposure during the 2022 episode, average | 0.349x | **0.521x** |
| Local exposure peak | 0.404x | **0.723x** (2020-03-12) |
| Local exposure, 20 sessions after each episode | 0.34-0.36x | **0.21-0.24x**, low 0.09x |

So the candidate holds **21-49% more local exposure during high-volatility episodes**, front-loaded
into the first days. Then it holds **about a third less for twenty sessions afterwards**, while the
hold-20 layers rebuild. It is a timing reallocation of local capital, not a change of horizon at
fixed risk.

**Gross and cash sanity for B:**

- **Close gross.** Max 0.811x on 2022-05-19, as reported. No end-of-day negative cash (minimum
  `$12.5k`).
- **After the morning entries** (the measure I introduced in 6.95), peak gross is **1.236x** —
  base 1.055x — and above 1.0x on 97 days, against 85.
- **Cash right after entries** falls to **−`$22.8k`, −23.6% of equity**, on 2022-05-23. Base's
  worst was −5.3%. **The intraday margin need is 4.5 times base's.**
- **Caps.** The gross cap never binds, and the ticker cap never binds on new orders. But held
  exposure in one name reaches **42.1% (BA, 2020-03-12)**, past the nominal 40%. Base B peaked
  at 39.3%.

**For A:** close max 0.930x. After entries, peak gross 1.408x on 194 days and cash **−40.8% of
equity**. The ticker cap binds on 285 trades (the same count as base), and held BA exposure
reaches 47.7%.

6.98's claim that "B remains operationally cleaner" still holds against A, but B-candidate is
materially less clean than B-base.

#### 5. Is the improvement real, or an artifact?

**The rule fires on only 57 of 1,665 sessions, in three episodes:**

- 2020-03-05 → 2020-05-05 (43 sessions);
- 2022-05-16 → 2022-06-02 (13 sessions);
- 2022-06-27 (1 session).

It never fires in 2018, 2019, 2021, 2023 or 2024.

**About half the gain is compounding.** Measured as return on start-of-year equity, the candidate
is identical to base in every year without a trigger — for B: 25.885% in 2021, 29.118% in 2023,
22.422% in 2024. The extra dollars in those years are the same return on a larger account. Only
2020 (41.84% against 39.11%) and 2022 (+0.09% against −2.53%) differ. Of B's +`$7.50k`, **+`$4.07k`
is earned in the trigger windows** (with their exit tails) and **+`$3.43k` is compounding
afterwards**.

**Horizon against size, B:**

| Variant | Local on trigger days | P&L | DD | Sharpe | 2020 return | 2022 return |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Base | hold 20, 1× notional | `$109.48k` | `−$15.44k` | 1.256 | 39.11% | −2.53% |
| **Horizon only** | hold 5, 1× notional | **`$105.85k`** | `−$13.94k` | 1.272 | 34.44% | −1.44% |
| **Size only** | hold 20, 4× notional | `$126.41k` | `−$19.40k` | 1.157 | `$33.51k` in dollars | `−$4.99k` in dollars |
| Candidate | hold 5, 4× notional | `$116.98k` | `−$15.89k` | 1.280 | 41.84% | +0.09% |

For A, horizon-only is `$131.09k` against base `$135.82k`.

- **At unchanged notional, the shorter exit costs `$3.6k` on B and `$4.7k` on A.** It helps 2022
  a little but gives up 4.7 points in 2020, where hold-20 caught the April rebound.
- **Adding size alone earns `$16.9k`**, at the price of Sharpe 1.157, drawdown −`$19.4k`, max gross
  1.52x and a worse 2022.
- **The candidate sits between the two.** It is the size-up, with the 5-day exit acting as the brake
  on its risk. That is the opposite of 6.97's reading that "changing the exit horizon beats simple
  size throttling".

**Threshold neighbourhood, B, same rule:**

| SPY vol threshold | Trigger dates | P&L | Sharpe | 2022 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.50% | 224 | `$108.62k` | 1.216 | `−$2.46k` |
| 1.75% | 129 | `$104.77k` | 1.203 | `−$3.69k` |
| **2.00%** | **55** | **`$116.98k`** | **1.280** | **`+$0.09k`** |
| 2.25% | 39 | `$115.97k` | 1.264 | `−$2.72k` |
| 2.50% | 36 | `$115.50k` | 1.262 | `−$2.72k` |

- **The "2022 fix" exists at exactly 2.0%.** At 2.25%, 2022 is worse than base. The May-June 2022
  episode crosses 2.0% and not 2.25%.
- **The total-P&L gain survives above 2%** only because of the COVID episode.
- **Below 2% the rule loses to base.**
- **The same action under every other trigger in the 6.97 sweep also loses to base:** bear_stack
  `$106.1k`, below_ma50 `$105.7k`, prev_down_1 `$107.5k`.

So the result rests on one threshold and, effectively, two volatility episodes.

#### 6. Side effects and git

- **No change during the audit.** Every Polygon artifact, script and pickle carries the same
  sha256 at the end as at the start.
- **Nothing deleted.** 21 cache pickles and 10 research parquet files present.
- **Codex's files.** The four scripts in `raits/research/`, which is untracked as a whole, and
  their CSV outputs, which git ignores. Ownership is therefore by modification time: the overlay
  sweep 08:28-08:48, the refine sweep 08:52-10:07, the runner 10:26 and its outputs 10:28 local —
  all consistent with 6.96-6.98.
- **Older outputs untouched.** No 6.91 or 6.92 output was modified.
- **Git status.** The tracked modified files are unchanged and unrelated: `SCRATCHPAD.md`,
  `TASK.md` and `monitor/paper_pnl_compare.json`.

#### 7. What to test next

1. **Out-of-sample episodes. This is the decisive test, and 2016-2017 warmup will not provide it.**
   SPY's previous-session 20-day volatility peaks at 1.71% in February-March 2018 and 1.54% in Q4
   2018. So scoring 2018 as a full year adds **no new trigger**. The warmup is still worth doing
   for the partial-2018 caveat, but it cannot test this rule. The rule needs volatility episodes
   it was not chosen on. Candidates are pre-2018 history — whether the 2008-2009, 2011 or 2015-2016
   selloffs cross 2% is not yet measured — or the sealed period when it is opened. That points at
   the survivorship-aware history build, which should come first anyway. **Pre-register the
   threshold, hold and sizing before looking.**
2. **Publish the sizing ladder with the candidate:** base, horizon-only, size-only and candidate,
   side by side. Add an exposure-matched variant — hold 5, with local notional set so that local
   exposure through each episode equals base. That is the only version whose result can be
   attributed to the exit horizon.
3. **Report the threshold curve (1.5%-3.0%)** and withdraw the "nearly neutralizes 2022" claim
   unless it survives on it. On current evidence it does not.
4. **Put post-entry gross, post-entry cash and held single-ticker exposure into the runner's
   outputs.**

**Bootstrap and concentration on this challenger are low value.** A rule that acts in two episodes
cannot be judged by resampling days.

Blockers before any lead change to this candidate:

- two effective episodes, chosen in-sample;
- 2022 improvement exists at one threshold only;
- gain requires a 4× notional that raises intraday margin to 24% of equity on B;
- plus everything already open for base: survivor universe, 2023-2024 already opened, partial
  2018, concentration.

#### Labels, kept separate

**Verified — I ran it and have my own number:**

- the runner hash and byte-identical reproduction of all four outputs;
- every expected summary and yearly figure, and B equal to the 6.97 probe;
- the 550-row signal diff with nothing else changed;
- the SPY flag reproduced independently;
- 490 of 550 exits on the true 5th session;
- 57 trigger sessions in three episodes;
- identical returns in every non-trigger year, and the `$4.07k` / `$3.43k` split;
- horizon-only, size-only and threshold-neighbourhood results for B, and horizon-only for A;
- local exposure paths and notionals;
- post-entry gross and cash, and held-ticker exposure;
- the rank of the winner in the 6.97 sweep;
- SPY vol maxima in 2018;
- no ML, no intraday, no Databento, no off-limits reference, and no artifact changed.

**Grounded suspicion — read the path, did not isolate:** that the two winning episodes share one
feature — a sharp V-shaped rebound after the trigger — which a front-loaded size-up exploits and
which will not recur on schedule.

**Nobody has run it:**

- an exposure-matched hold-5 variant;
- the rule on any volatility episode outside 2020 and 2022;
- whether pre-2018 selloffs cross the 2% threshold;
- any of this on a survivorship-aware universe.

Why `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40` remains lead:

- It has the cleanest operating profile: maxGross 0.677x, no cash-negative days in the 6.93 sanity
  table, and the month-block bootstrap p01 is `$36.860k`.
- It survives cost/cap stress: at 24 bps with ticker cap 40%, it still earns `$47.769k`.
- Its weakness is transparent: 2022 is negative because broad/local hold20 are long-biased in bear
  down legs, while YDAY offsets much of the loss.
- It does not depend on the high-vol threshold/hold interaction found in-sample.

Why A is not lead despite higher PnL:

- A and B are the same book at different gross levels.
- A earns more, but uses more gross and has larger DD. Sharpe is effectively the same as B.
- A remains useful as the higher-gross reference, not the cleaner operating default.

Why the hold5 high-vol variant is not promoted:

- The attractive version (`hold5_engine_sizing`) improves PnL because changing hold20 to hold5 also
  increases local daily budget through the engine's `sleeve_gross / hold` sizing.
- The fair-sizing version isolates the exit-horizon effect: `B_polygon62_hold5_fixed_hold20_sizing`
  improves DD and Sharpe but reduces total PnL from `$109.480k` to `$105.855k`.
- The rule triggers in too few high-vol episodes and was selected after looking at the same
  2018-2024 survivor-62 sample.
- Therefore it is research-only until tested on pre-registered out-of-sample volatility episodes and
  preferably a survivorship-aware universe.

Current verdicts:

| item | verdict |
|---|---|
| ML sleeve | Headline FAIL / research-only |
| `intraday_ex10` | FAIL for Polygon-62 2018-2024 one-engine |
| `A_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40` | WARN, higher-gross reference |
| `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40` | WARN+, current lead |
| `B_polygon62_hold5_engine_sizing` | WARN / research-only tactical variant |
| Production PASS | Not yet |

Next useful work:

1. Build/fetch a survivorship-aware or at least historically wider universe.
2. Add 2016-2017 warmup if continuing with Polygon data so 2018 can be measured as a full calendar
   year.
3. Pre-register any high-vol hold/sizing rule before testing on new volatility episodes.
4. Keep the official lead as `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40` until those tests pass.

| B | hold-10 fixed hold-20 sizing | `$104.960k` | `-$13.137k` | 1.204 | 0.681x | `-$1.431k` |

Verdict:

- Keep official lead as `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40`.
- Warmup did not make 2018 positive.
- The hold5-vol20 interpretation is unchanged: the engine-sizing version improves headline PnL,
  but the fixed-sizing variant reduces total PnL while improving DD/Sharpe. This remains a
  risk-shaping diagnostic / research-only tactical idea, not a promoted lead.
- Main blocker remains unchanged: current-survivor Polygon-62 is not survivorship-aware.

### 6.105 Post-selection ticker drop diagnostic

The 6.104 concentration table is attribution, not a removal simulation. It answers where realized
closed-trade PnL came from. It does not answer what happens if a ticker is banned and the sleeve
budget is reallocated to the remaining signals.

This first diagnostic filters ticker(s) out of the already-built signal table before simulation,
then lets the same one-engine sizing allocate each sleeve's daily budget across the remaining
already-selected names.

Important limitation: this is not a full universe rerun. It does not promote local rank 11 into the
local top 10, does not promote the next broad candidate into the broad selection, and does not WFO
YDAY again after the ticker ban. It is therefore a post-selection drop diagnostic, not the final
counterfactual.

Outputs:

- `STOCKS_POLYGON62_B_LEAD_COUNTERFACTUAL_DROP_REPLACEMENT_2016WARMUP_2018_2024.csv`
- `STOCKS_POLYGON62_B_LEAD_COUNTERFACTUAL_DROP_REPLACEMENT_YEARLY_2016WARMUP_2018_2024.csv`

Portfolio: `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40`, 2016-09 warmup, 2018-2024 scoring.

| case | dropped | PnL | delta vs base | DD | Sharpe | avgGross | maxGross | trades |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base | none | `$107.082k` | `$0.000k` | `-$14.216k` | 1.193 | 0.603x | 0.681x | 32,767 |
| drop TSLA | TSLA | `$74.077k` | `-$33.005k` | `-$17.506k` | 0.992 | 0.603x | 0.682x | 31,927 |
| drop top 3 | TSLA, NVDA, PANW | `$58.454k` | `-$48.628k` | `-$20.410k` | 0.841 | 0.601x | 0.672x | 30,780 |
| drop top 5 | TSLA, NVDA, PANW, NOW, INTU | `$49.093k` | `-$57.989k` | `-$19.866k` | 0.754 | 0.592x | 0.671x | 29,788 |
| drop top 10 | TSLA, NVDA, PANW, NOW, INTU, AMAT, BA, ORCL, AVGO, LOW | `$33.869k` | `-$73.213k` | `-$18.857k` | 0.576 | 0.578x | 0.673x | 27,025 |
| drop bottom 5 | INTC, MU, AMD, PFE, C | `$128.313k` | `+$21.231k` | `-$14.031k` | 1.433 | 0.602x | 0.682x | 29,500 |

Read:

- Replacement fill helps, but it does not remove the concentration risk. After removing TSLA,
  the system still loses about `$33.0k` versus base.
- Removing the top 5 positive tickers leaves the book profitable, but cuts PnL by about `$58.0k`
  and drops Sharpe from 1.193 to 0.754.
- Removing the bottom 5 detractors improves the book materially. That is not a deployable rule by
  itself because the bad tickers are selected in-sample, but it shows ticker-level selection matters
  a lot.
- 6.104 should be read as attribution; 6.105 should be read only as a post-selection drop
  diagnostic.

### 6.106 Full universe-rerun ticker drop counterfactual

After 6.105, I reran the more correct replacement test: remove tickers before sleeve generation,
then rebuild broad, local and YDAY selections before the one-engine simulation.

This means:

- broad reselects from the remaining universe;
- local rank 11 can become rank 10 after a banned ticker is removed;
- YDAY WFO is rerun without the banned ticker(s);
- engine sizing then runs normally.

| case | dropped | PnL | delta vs base | DD | Sharpe | avgGross | maxGross | trades |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base rerun | none | `$107.082k` | `$0.000k` | `-$14.216k` | 1.193 | 0.603x | 0.681x | 32,767 |
| drop TSLA | TSLA | `$69.848k` | `-$37.234k` | `-$15.829k` | 0.940 | 0.613x | 0.678x | 32,475 |
| drop top 3 | TSLA, NVDA, PANW | `$60.732k` | `-$46.350k` | `-$16.584k` | 0.848 | 0.605x | 0.675x | 32,006 |
| drop top 5 | TSLA, NVDA, PANW, NOW, INTU | `$53.600k` | `-$53.482k` | `-$15.481k` | 0.783 | 0.598x | 0.672x | 31,467 |
| drop top 10 | TSLA, NVDA, PANW, NOW, INTU, AMAT, BA, ORCL, AVGO, LOW | `$52.714k` | `-$54.368k` | `-$11.139k` | 0.778 | 0.603x | 0.675x | 30,164 |

Selection counts:

| case | broad rows | local rows | YDAY rows | final signals/trades |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base rerun | 15,288 | 17,250 | 415 | 32,767 |
| drop TSLA | 15,071 | 17,250 | 245 | 32,475 |
| drop top 3 | 14,607 | 17,250 | 235 | 32,006 |
| drop top 5 | 14,087 | 17,250 | 213 | 31,467 |
| drop top 10 | 12,804 | 17,250 | 183 | 30,164 |

Read:

- The user's objection to 6.105 was correct: post-selection deletion is not enough to answer the
  replacement question.
- Full refill improves the top-10 deletion result versus post-selection deletion (`$52.714k`
  instead of `$33.869k`), showing that replacement candidates do matter.
- But replacement candidates do not erase the concentration risk. Dropping TSLA still costs
  `$37.234k` relative to base after full sleeve reruns.
- The main reason is not that every replacement is loss-making; it is that the replacements are
  lower-ranked by the same rules and do not reproduce the removed names' realized edge, especially
  the large TSLA/NVDA/PANW YDAY contributions.
- The full-refill test reinforces rather than weakens the concentration caveat: the book remains
  profitable without top names, but the headline Sharpe/PnL depend heavily on them.

### 6.107 Survivorship-aware universe build plan

The next production-blocker workstream is not another candidate search. It is building a
point-in-time, survivorship-aware equity universe.

Plan document:

- `STOCKS_SURVIVORSHIP_AWARE_UNIVERSE_PLAN_2026-09-12.md`

Core principle:

- Every universe, feature, signal and trade row must carry a stable `security_id`.
- Ticker is a date-ranged attribute, not identity.
- Universe membership must be decided using only information available as of that date.

Required tables:

- `security_master.parquet`
- `ticker_history.parquet`
- `corporate_actions.parquet`
- `daily_universe.parquet`
- `market_data_coverage.parquet`

Proposed build phases:

1. Requirements freeze.
2. Source evaluation.
3. Security master and ticker map.
4. Daily PIT universe.
5. Market data binding.
6. Feature pipeline integration.
7. Sleeve regeneration.
8. One-engine replay and comparison versus current-survivor Polygon-62.

Recommended immediate next step:

- Build a small prototype schema with 5-10 securities before buying/fetching bulk data:
  a stable survivor, a ticker rename such as FB/META, a major split name, a delisted/acquired name,
  and a multiple-share-class issuer.

No strategy parameter should be changed for this workstream. The first PIT run should answer only
whether the current fixed no-ML lead survives a more realistic historical universe.

### 6.108 Independent audit of concentration and full-refill tests

Independent audit summary supplied after 6.104-6.107. The audit was read-only and did not modify
repo files.

Findings:

- No wrong numbers were found in 6.104 or 6.106.
- 6.104 attribution reconciles closed-trade PnL to equity PnL within `1e-9`.
- 6.104 ticker and sleeve figures match independently rebuilt calculations:
  - TSLA `$26.587k`, 24.8% of total PnL.
  - Top 3 tickers 41.0%.
  - Top 5 tickers 51.3%.
  - Top 10 tickers 68.6%.
  - Sleeve figures match, and the by-ticker file matches within `1e-12`.
- 6.106 full-refill rerun matches independently rebuilt results to the cent for PnL, drawdown,
  Sharpe, trades and broad/local/YDAY row counts.
- No trade from a dropped ticker leaks through the full-refill cases.

Provenance warning:

- The numeric outputs for 6.104-6.106 were produced by ad hoc harnesses in-session.
- No retained script in the allowed research tree regenerates all 6.104-6.106 outputs end to end.
- Therefore the numbers are audit-confirmed but provenance is `WARN` until the harness is retained
  as a script.

Interpretation adjustments:

- YDAY's row drop after removing TSLA is real, not a bug. Without TSLA in training history, WFO
  chooses stricter rules:
  - rolling 2021 changes `raw_-6` to `raw_-7`;
  - rolling 2022 changes `gapdown_-4` to `raw_-6`;
  - anchored 2023-2024 changes to `quality_-5_gapdown_mompos`.
- Therefore full-refill deltas mix two effects: replacement names and WFO rule re-selection.
- Audit rerun with base YDAY rules frozen:

| case | post-selection | refill with frozen rules | full refill |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Drop TSLA | `$74.1k` | `$78.1k` | `$69.8k` |
| Drop top 10 | `$33.9k` | `$44.2k` | `$52.7k` |

Read:

- Rule re-selection is material: about `-$8.2k` for the TSLA drop and `+$8.5k` for the top-10 drop.
- Claims such as "top 10 is close to top 5" or "replacement rescues top 10" are partly WFO rule
  behavior, not pure ticker replacement.
- Dropping TSLA costs more than TSLA's direct attribution because the book compounds. Removing an
  early winner shrinks later capital; attribution understates TSLA's effective weight.
- The apparent better dollar drawdown in removal cases is mostly a smaller-account artifact.
  Percentage max drawdown is broadly similar: base about `-20.7%`, removal cases about `-18.6%` to
  `-19.5%`.
- CAGR is the cleaner concentration read:
  - base 17.8%;
  - without TSLA 13.3%;
  - without top 3 12.0%;
  - without top 5 11.0%;
  - without top 10 10.8%.

Residual caveats:

- Local refill works as intended: local stays at 17,250 rows; TSLA's 538 local rows are replaced by
  exactly 538 rank-11 names on those dates.
- TSLA provides `$22.2k` of its `$26.6k` through YDAY, from 41 trades. That is 56.8% of YDAY's PnL.
- 6.105 is correctly labelled as post-selection diagnostic in text, but the file name contains
  `COUNTERFACTUAL_DROP_REPLACEMENT`; that file name overstates what it does.
- The 6.105 `drop_bottom5` result is in-sample ticker picking and was not rerun as full refill.

Audit verdict:

- Implementation of 6.104-6.106: `PASS` on numbers.
- Provenance: `WARN`.
- Lead remains `WARN+`, not production `PASS`.
- Main blockers remain current-survivor universe and concentration.
- The survivorship-aware test should also freeze or explicitly pre-register the WFO rule-selection
  protocol, because removing names changes which YDAY rules the walk-forward picks.

Question: does a simple pyramid/add-on rule improve the current lead beyond a plain gross-up?

- `raits/research/stocks_polygon62_pyramid_diagnostic_2016warmup.py`

Outputs:

- `STOCKS_POLYGON62_B_LEAD_PYRAMID_DIAGNOSTIC_SUMMARY_2016WARMUP_2018_2024.csv`
- `STOCKS_POLYGON62_B_LEAD_PYRAMID_DIAGNOSTIC_YEARLY_2016WARMUP_2018_2024.csv`
- `STOCKS_POLYGON62_B_LEAD_PYRAMID_DIAGNOSTIC_TRADES_2016WARMUP_2018_2024.csv`

Rule tested:

- Base portfolio: `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40`.
- Pyramiding allowed only on `broad_adv10_g2_dd85` and `local_xs_full_s10`.
- No pyramiding on `yday_ex6_actual`.
- Add after 5 trading days if open-to-entry unrealized return is at least +5%.
- Add size is 25% of the parent trade's original notional.
- Maximum one add per parent trade.
- Same planned exit date as parent.
- Same 40% ticker cap and 1.75 gross cap.
- Add-ons are entered before same-day new base signals, so they consume gross capacity.

Controls:

- `B_base_repro`: reproduce base B.
- `B_gross037_control`: same book, all sleeve weights 0.37 instead of 0.35.
- `B_gross040_control`: same book, all sleeve weights 0.40 instead of 0.35; this reproduces A
  no-intraday economics under B naming.

Summary:

| case | PnL | CAGR | DD | Sharpe | avgGross | maxGross | trades | add-ons | 2022 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `B_base_repro` | `$107.082k` | 17.8% | `-$14.216k` | 1.193 | 0.603x | 0.681x | 32,767 | 0 | `-$2.327k` |
| `B_pyramid_d5_r5_add25` | `$112.145k` | 18.3% | `-$15.360k` | 1.179 | 0.637x | 0.740x | 47,742 | 14,975 | `-$3.322k` |
| `B_pyramid_local_d5_r7p5_add15_cap20` | `$108.103k` | 17.9% | `-$14.472k` | 1.189 | 0.610x | 0.688x | 38,405 | 5,638 | `-$2.549k` |
| `B_pyramid_local_d5_r5_add20_hold5` | `$107.085k` | 17.8% | `-$14.418k` | 1.186 | 0.609x | 0.685x | 40,893 | 8,126 | `-$2.600k` |
| `B_pyramid_broad_local_d5_r5_add20_hold5` | `$107.624k` | 17.8% | `-$14.519k` | 1.184 | 0.613x | 0.692x | 47,742 | 14,975 | `-$2.821k` |
| `B_gross037_control` | `$116.914k` | 18.8% | `-$15.622k` | 1.192 | 0.637x | 0.720x | 32,767 | 0 | `-$2.671k` |
| `B_gross040_control` | `$132.295k` | 20.3% | `-$17.863k` | 1.189 | 0.688x | 0.777x | 32,767 | 0 | `-$3.263k` |

Add-on attribution:

| add-on sleeve | add-on trades | add-on closed PnL | avg PnL/add |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `broad_adv10_g2_dd85` | 6,849 | `$1.364k` | `$0.20` |
| `local_xs_full_s10` | 8,126 | `$1.983k` | `$0.24` |
| total | 14,975 | `$3.347k` | `$0.22` |

Additional pyramid variants:

| variant | add-on rule | add-on trades | add-on PnL | read |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| `local_d5_r7p5_add15_cap20` | local only, +7.5%, add 15%, ticker add cap 20% | 5,638 | `$0.732k` | much less exposure, but almost no improvement |
| `local_d5_r5_add20_hold5` | local only, +5%, add 20%, add-on exits after 5 sessions | 8,126 | `$0.280k` | flat versus base |
| `broad_local_d5_r5_add20_hold5` | broad+local, +5%, add 20%, add-on exits after 5 sessions | 14,975 | `$0.676k` | small PnL lift, worse Sharpe/2022 |

Read:

- The base reproduction matches the warmup lead exactly.
- The pyramid rule adds `$5.063k` of portfolio PnL versus base, but Sharpe falls from 1.193 to
  1.179 and drawdown worsens from `-$14.216k` to `-$15.360k`.
- A simple gross-up to 0.37 sleeve weights beats pyramid on PnL and Sharpe at nearly the same
  average gross: `$116.914k`, Sharpe 1.192, avgGross 0.637x.
- Tighter or shorter-hold pyramid variants do not solve the issue. They reduce extra exposure, but
  the edge mostly disappears.
- Pyramid creates many extra trades: 14,975 add-ons, taking total trades to 47,742 and max active
  positions to 601.
- 2022 gets worse under pyramid: `-$3.322k` versus base `-$2.327k`.
- This is not a promoted candidate. It is a diagnostic showing that this simple winner-add rule
  mostly behaves like a noisier gross increase.

Verdict:

- Pyramid diagnostic: `FAIL` as lead improvement.
- Keep official lead unchanged: `B_polygon62_no_intraday_cap40`.
- If pyramiding is revisited later, it should be tested only after survivorship-aware data and with
  stricter pre-registered operational constraints.

### 6.111 Polygon source capability probe for PIT universe

Question: can Polygon support the survivorship-aware PIT universe workstream, at least for a small
real-source smoke sample?

Retained script:

- `raits/research/stocks_pit_source_probe_polygon.py`

This is a small API capability probe only. It is not a bulk fetch and not a strategy result.

Outputs:

- `STOCKS_PIT_SOURCE_PROBE_POLYGON_20260912_SUMMARY.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_SOURCE_PROBE_POLYGON_20260912_DETAILS.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_SOURCE_PROBE_POLYGON_20260912_REFERENCE_SEARCH.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_SOURCE_PROBE_POLYGON_20260912_SPLITS.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_SOURCE_PROBE_POLYGON_20260912_AGGS.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_SOURCE_PROBE_POLYGON_20260912_UNIVERSE_PAGES.csv`
- `raits/data/cache/stocks_survivorship/source_probe_polygon/manifest_20260912.json`

Probe cases:

- AAPL stable survivor.
- FB on 2022-06-08 and META on 2022-06-09.
- TWTR on 2022-10-27 and 2022-10-28, plus inactive reference search.
- NVDA split references in 2021 and 2024.
- GOOG/GOOGL share classes and split references.
- TWTR daily adjusted bars around delisting.
- First page of active common-stock reference universe by historical date.

Capability summary:

| capability | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| stable security identifier | PARTIAL | details expose `composite_figi` and `share_class_figi`; delisted coverage needs audit |
| ticker rename PIT details | PASS | FB/META date-specific details queried |
| delisted ticker reference | PASS | TWTR `active=false` reference search returns a delisted row |
| split reference | PASS | NVDA and GOOG/GOOGL split references returned |
| delisted market data smoke | PASS | TWTR adjusted daily bars available through 2022-10-27 |
| active common universe page | PASS | reference tickers endpoint returns paginated active common-stock pages by date |
| production PIT sufficiency | WARN | full pagination, delisted identity and durable `security_id` policy still need validation |

Concrete probe findings:

- FB on 2022-06-08 returns ticker `FB`, CIK `0001326801`, composite FIGI `BBG000MM2P62`,
  share-class FIGI `BBG001SQCQC5`.
- META on 2022-06-09 returns ticker `META` with the same CIK and FIGIs as FB. This is promising for
  bridging the rename with stable identity fields.
- TWTR `active=false` reference search returns one inactive common-stock row with delisted metadata
  fields present.
- TWTR adjusted daily aggregates for 2022-10-24 through 2022-11-04 return four bars only:
  2022-10-24 through 2022-10-27. That matches delisting behavior.
- NVDA split references return:
  - 2021-07-20, `1 -> 4`;
  - 2024-06-10, `1 -> 10`.
- GOOGL and GOOG split references return 2022-07-18, `1 -> 20`.
- Active common-stock universe page queries for 2022-06-08 and 2022-10-27 return 1,000 rows with
  `next_url` present, implying full pagination is required.

Important caveat:

- `ticker details` for TWTR with `date=2022-10-28` still returned `active=True`, while the
  `active=false` reference endpoint identifies TWTR as inactive/delisted. A PIT builder must not
  trust a single `details(date).active` field blindly. It needs a documented precedence rule using
  ticker reference rows, delisted fields, market-data coverage and ticker history.

Read:

- Polygon appears viable enough for a **next smoke prototype** using real rows and pagination.
- Polygon is not yet proven sufficient for production PIT. The open questions are stable identity
  across all delisted rows, full pagination correctness, ticker-history edge cases and intraday
  coverage for delisted names.
- Next step should be a small paginated real-source builder for the same prototype cases, not a
  bulk universe fetch.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

QA:

- Ticker is unique within each snapshot date: PASS for all four dates.
- All rows are `type=CS` and active: PASS for all four dates.
- Pagination completed: PASS, 6 pages per date.
- Share-class FIGI uniqueness: PASS except 2022-06-09.

Duplicate identity rows on 2022-06-09:

| date | tickers | name / event | shared FIGI |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022-06-09 | FB, META | Meta Platforms rename overlap | `BBG001SQCQC5` |
| 2022-06-09 | RLGY, HOUS | Realogy / Anywhere rename overlap | `BBG001SSDCC1` |

Read:

- Polygon can provide paginated active common-stock snapshots by historical date.
- Raw snapshots cannot be used directly as PIT universe membership because rename effective dates
  can contain two active tickers for the same share-class FIGI.
- This is not a fatal blocker; it is exactly the kind of identity-resolution rule the PIT builder
  must implement.

Required resolver before bulk fetch:

1. Build identity groups by `share_class_figi` when present, else `composite_figi`, else a fallback
   source id.
2. For a same-date duplicate identity group, prefer the ticker whose date-ranged ticker history is
   valid on that date.
3. If ticker history is not yet known, query details/aggs around the event and choose the ticker
   with market bars on that date; keep the other as an alias/overlap row, not a second security.
4. Emit a QA table of every duplicate identity group and the chosen canonical ticker for that date.

Next step:

- Implement a small resolver on these four snapshot dates and verify that FB/META and RLGY/HOUS
  collapse to one `security_id` per date before attempting a broader historical universe build.

### 6.114 Polygon snapshot identity resolver smoke test

Implemented the retained resolver requested by 6.113.

Retained script:

- `raits/research/stocks_pit_polygon_snapshot_resolver.py`

Input directories:

- `raits/data/cache/stocks_survivorship/polygon_universe_snapshot/`

Output directory:

- `raits/data/cache/stocks_survivorship/polygon_universe_resolved_sample/`

Parquet outputs:

- `resolved_universe_snapshot.parquet`
- `duplicate_identity_resolutions.parquet`
- `duplicate_identity_event_evidence.parquet`
- `resolved_daily_counts.parquet`
- `manifest_20260912.json`

Report outputs:

- `STOCKS_PIT_POLYGON_UNIVERSE_RESOLVED_20260912_ROWS.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_POLYGON_UNIVERSE_RESOLVED_20260912_DUPLICATE_RESOLUTIONS.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_POLYGON_UNIVERSE_RESOLVED_20260912_EVENT_EVIDENCE.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_POLYGON_UNIVERSE_RESOLVED_20260912_DAILY_COUNTS.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_POLYGON_UNIVERSE_RESOLVED_20260912_QA_SUMMARY.csv`

Resolver rule:

- Use `share_class_figi` as the primary identity key.
- Fall back to `composite_figi`, then `CIK+ticker`, then `ticker`.
- For duplicate `(date, identity_key)` groups, prefer a ticker that is valid in sampled ticker
  history for that date, then one with Polygon event-window daily bars on the duplicate date,
  then one with sampled daily bars for that date, then a deterministic `last_updated_utc` /
  ticker tie-break.
- Event evidence is cached to `duplicate_identity_event_evidence.parquet`; reruns use the cache
  when it covers the duplicate rows.

QA:

| check | status | detail |
|---|---|---|
| resolved identity unique by date | PASS | 0 duplicate `(date, identity_key)` rows after resolution |
| duplicate groups recorded | PASS | 2 groups, 2 dropped duplicate rows |
| FB/META resolved to META on 2022-06-09 | PASS | chosen via sampled ticker history and daily bar |
| HOUS/RLGY resolved by event bar | PASS | HOUS `event_daily_bar+event_detail_identity` |

Daily counts:

| date | raw rows | resolved rows | dropped duplicate identity rows |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2022-06-08 | 5,845 | 5,845 | 0 |
| 2022-06-09 | 5,846 | 5,844 | 2 |
| 2022-10-27 | 5,784 | 5,784 | 0 |
| 2022-10-28 | 5,783 | 5,783 | 0 |

Duplicate resolutions:

| date | identity key | tickers | chosen | reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022-06-09 | `SHARE_FIGI:BBG001SQCQC5` | FB, META | META | sample ticker history + event daily bar + sample daily bar + event detail identity |
| 2022-06-09 | `SHARE_FIGI:BBG001SSDCC1` | HOUS, RLGY | HOUS | event daily bar + event detail identity |

Event evidence:

| date | ticker | event bar present | first bar in event window | last bar in event window |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 2022-06-09 | FB | false | 2022-06-06 | 2022-06-08 |
| 2022-06-09 | META | true | 2022-06-09 | 2022-06-14 |
| 2022-06-09 | HOUS | true | 2022-06-09 | 2022-06-14 |
| 2022-06-09 | RLGY | false | 2022-06-06 | 2022-06-08 |

Read:

- The resolver collapses known rename-overlap rows to one identity per date.
- FB/META is resolved from actual sampled history plus event-window market-data presence.
- HOUS/RLGY is now resolved from event-window market-data presence, not fallback.
- Polygon detail still marks both old and new tickers active on the duplicate date, so the
  event-window bar check is the useful discriminator for same-FIGI rename overlaps.

### 6.121 Full-daily PIT scale plan and resumable builder

Before launching the long 2018-2024 daily PIT universe build, added a resumable wrapper around the
Polygon universe builder.

Retained script:

- `raits/research/stocks_pit_polygon_daily_universe_resumable.py`

Why:

- Full daily 2018-2024 is the slowest remaining part of this step.
- Expected size is roughly 1,800 trading dates and about 6 Polygon pages per date.
- A monolithic run is fragile because an interruption late in the run would waste hours unless each
  date has explicit resume state.

Resumable behavior:

- `--mode fetch` fetches/caches one date at a time into the same `raw_snapshots/` and
  `page_manifests/` layout used by the existing builder.
- `resumable_status.csv` records `date`, `status`, `rows`, `pages`, elapsed seconds, attempts and
  error text.
- Reruns skip dates already marked `OK` with complete pagination.
- `--mode assemble` refuses to assemble if any target date is missing/incomplete.
- `--mode assemble` then concatenates raw/page caches, runs duplicate identity resolution,
  instrument cleaning and QA, and writes the same parquet/CSV output family as the bulk builder.
- It keeps the existing hard guard against opening dates after 2024-12-31.

Smoke test:

- Ran cached `fetch-assemble` on the already fetched 2022-06-06 to 2022-06-07 transition subset.
- Restored the full 2022-06-06 to 2022-06-14 transition aggregate immediately after the smoke test.
- Full transition aggregate is back to 7 dates, pagination PASS, 2 duplicate groups and 2 dropped
  rows.

Current step status:

| substep | status | notes |
|---|---|---|
| PIT source probe | DONE | Polygon viable enough for prototype; production still needs QA |
| real-source sample | DONE | FB/META, TWTR, GOOG/GOOGL, NVDA sample tables built |
| snapshot pagination | DONE | monthly and event windows paginate correctly |
| identity resolver | DONE | duplicate same-FIGI rename overlaps collapse correctly |
| instrument cleaning | DONE | funds/preferreds/units/warrants/rights excluded, trust names still policy WARN |
| monthly liquidity diagnostic | DONE | useful diagnostic, but monthly cannot precisely handle mid-month transitions |
| limited full-daily transition QA | DONE | ticker carry-over PASS; TWTR stale-active bug fixed by current-day bar requirement |
| full daily universe fetch | DONE | 1,826/1,826 business-calendar dates OK |
| full daily liquidity filter | DONE | QA PASS with WARN caveats for ambiguous tickers/fallback |
| PIT-to-strategy replay wiring | PENDING | no strategy replay before daily universe + liquidity QA pass |

Remaining steps for this PIT data step:

1. Wire the PIT eligible universe into a strategy replay.

### 6.125 PIT-gated Polygon-62 replay and unadjusted liquidity correction

Follow-up replay wiring exposed and fixed two important PIT-gate issues before using the results.

Corrections:

- The first 6.124 liquidity artifact used Polygon grouped bars with `adjusted=true`. That is not
  valid for a historical tradability price floor because split-adjusted prices can push historical
  shares below `$5` even when their live market price was not below `$5`.
- `raits/research/stocks_pit_polygon_liquidity_filter.py` now supports `--unadjusted-bars` and a
  separate cache directory, `raits/data/cache/stocks_survivorship/polygon_grouped_daily_unadjusted/`.
- The PIT replay gate initially matched only `(date, ticker)`. That incorrectly dropped historical
  `META` rows before the FB/META rename because the current Polygon-62 signal cache uses modern
  ticker spelling. `raits/research/stocks_polygon62_pit_replay_2016warmup.py` now falls back through
  `security_id` alias matching; those rows are recorded as `security_alias`.

- The script now de-duplicates by symbol/month output file before worker submission. The original
  plan contained overlapping symbol/month rows from security-id history transitions; these are
  one API/month file and should not be fetched concurrently into the same parquet path.
- Temporary parquet writes now use process/thread-specific temp filenames.
- Worker exceptions are caught and logged instead of terminating the whole batch loop.

Fetch commands used after the initial single-worker batches:

- `python raits/research/stocks_pit_full_5min_fetch.py --max-chunks 10000 --workers 30 --sleep 0.13 --retries 4`
- `python raits/research/stocks_pit_full_5min_fetch.py --max-chunks 20000 --workers 30 --sleep 0.13 --retries 4`
- Repeated 30-worker batches until the script dry-run reported no pending work.

Completion status:

- Runtime fetch plan after symbol/month de-duplication: 176,028 chunks across 5,097 symbols.
- Dry-run resume check: `DONE 176,028`, `PENDING 0`.
- Parquet files present: 176,028.
- Parquet size: about 10.669 GB.
- Status CSV latest rows: 151,408 OK, 0 EMPTY, 0 latest ERROR.
- The status CSV has fewer OK rows than parquet files because one pre-patch concurrent batch hit a
  Windows file-lock after many workers had already written parquet files but before the main process
  appended all status rows. This is expected and not data loss: the resume rule explicitly treats
  existing non-empty parquet files as done, and the final dry-run confirmed zero pending chunks.

Interpretation:

- Broad PIT 5-minute market-data coverage is now available for the eligible universe.
- This completes the coverage-building substep; it does not yet produce broad PIT strategy stats.
- Next step is a coverage/integrity audit over the 176,028 parquet files, then true broad PIT
  replay/reselection with join QA and ambiguous-ticker/fallback impact reporting.

### 6.130 Broad PIT yday quality audit and first filtered rerun

Question tested:

> Is the broad PIT no-warmup replay much weaker because the broad universe lacks stock-quality filters,
> especially in the yday sleeve?

Scripts:

- `raits/research/stocks_pit_full_quality_audit_nowarmup.py`
- `raits/research/stocks_pit_full_yday_quality_variants_nowarmup.py`

Outputs:

- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_QUALITY_AUDIT_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_*`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_YDAY_QUALITY_VARIANTS_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_SUMMARY.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_YDAY_QUALITY_VARIANTS_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_YEARLY.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_YDAY_QUALITY_VARIANTS_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_SIGNAL_QA.csv`

The first pass was only diagnostic, joining executed trades from section 6.129 to PIT/daily quality
fields. It showed the broad and local sleeves should not receive blunt quality filters:

| sleeve | all PnL | price >= 10 PnL | vol20 <= 6% PnL | note |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| broad | `$16.540k` | `$14.540k` | `$17.125k` | mostly neutral/mixed |
| local | `$27.111k` | `$6.281k` | `$11.743k` | blunt quality filters destroy local edge |
| yday | `-$14.290k` | `-$3.855k` | `-$4.888k` | low-price/high-vol names drive much of the loss |

The yday losses are not simply "downtrend garbage." In the executed-trade diagnostic, `ret60 > -20%`
made yday much worse (`-$37.115k`). The worst broad-PIT yday damage is concentrated in volatile,
low-price, event-like names such as `NETE`, `GOVX`, `PACW`, `SRNE`, `FRC`, `GME`, `DM`, `TSP`, `SDC`,
`KODK`, `RKT`, `WE`, and `AMC`.

Then actual portfolio reruns were done with filters applied only to the `yday_ex6_actual` signals.
Broad and local signals were left unchanged. This is the important test because it lets the engine
refill/cap/recompound normally instead of subtracting old P&L mechanically.

Actual rerun summary:

| portfolio / yday filter | PnL | CAGR | DD | Sharpe | maxGross | trades | yday signals kept |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| B base | `$29.361k` | 7.1% | `-$23.691k` | 0.271 | 0.962x | 46,102 | 270 / 270 |
| B yday price >= 10 | `$46.127k` | 10.2% | `-$24.700k` | 0.416 | 0.894x | 46,025 | 193 / 270 |
| B yday price >= 15 | `$44.949k` | 10.0% | `-$24.402k` | 0.423 | 0.894x | 45,984 | 152 / 270 |
| B yday vol20 <= 6% | `$37.031k` | 8.5% | `-$23.129k` | 0.403 | 0.896x | 45,984 | 152 / 270 |
| B yday price >= 10 and vol20 <= 6% | `$39.586k` | 9.0% | `-$26.796k` | 0.413 | 0.895x | 45,960 | 128 / 270 |
| B yday price >= 15 and vol20 <= 6% | `$42.036k` | 9.4% | `-$31.597k` | 0.419 | 0.896x | 45,939 | 107 / 270 |

The A variants move similarly:

| portfolio / yday filter | PnL | CAGR | DD | Sharpe | maxGross |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A base | `$30.952k` | 7.4% | `-$27.503k` | 0.252 | 1.117x |
| A yday price >= 10 | `$51.400k` | 11.0% | `-$29.527k` | 0.399 | 1.017x |
| A yday price >= 15 | `$50.754k` | 10.9% | `-$29.541k` | 0.408 | 1.021x |
| A yday vol20 <= 6% | `$40.904k` | 9.2% | `-$27.244k` | 0.387 | 1.019x |

Interpretation:

- Yes, missing quality control is a material part of the broad PIT weakness, especially in yday.
- The cleanest first filter is not a complicated combo. `yday prior_close >= 10` is the strongest
  simple P&L repair for B (`$29.361k` -> `$46.127k`) and lifts Sharpe from 0.271 to 0.416, though DD
  worsens slightly from `-$23.691k` to `-$24.700k`.
- `yday vol20 <= 6%` is more conservative: smaller P&L repair (`$37.031k`) but slightly better DD
  than base (`-$23.129k`) and much better Sharpe (0.403).
- Combining price and vol filters is not automatically better. It reduces yday signals too far and
  can make drawdown worse due to different compounding/timing.
- Do **not** apply the same blunt filters to local. The local sleeve's broad-PIT edge lives in names
  that these filters remove.

Verdict:

- The broad PIT result remains WARN+, not production PASS.
- Keep `B yday price >= 10` and `B yday vol20 <= 6%` as new broad-PIT challenger variants.
- Do not promote either until:
  - 2016-2017 broad warmup is fetched/built for an apples-to-apples 2018-2024 scoring window;
  - ambiguous ticker fallback impact is audited;
  - the yday filter is pre-registered and rerun in a warmup-matched engine.

| total | `$107.082k` | `$29.361k` | `-$77.720k` |

So about two-thirds of the gap is yday alone. Broad and local degrade too, but they do not explain

This is not mainly a missing-January-to-March-2018 or missing-full-2016 issue. On the Polygon62
warmup run, removing entries before 2018-03-29 does **not** lower PnL:

| Polygon62 B slice | broad | local | yday | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| Entries from 2018-03-29 onward | `$31.902k` | `$37.551k` | `$39.136k` | `$108.589k` |

The omitted early-2018 Polygon62 entries were net negative. A warmup-matched broad PIT replay is
still needed for fairness, but it should not be expected to recover a `$77k` gap by itself.

Old-vs-new ticker split inside broad PIT:

| sleeve | ticker group | trades | PnL | avg PnL | win |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| broad | in Polygon62 | 9,737 | `$5.800k` | `$0.596` | 56.8% |
| broad | not in Polygon62 | 22,405 | `$10.740k` | `$0.479` | 52.4% |
| local | in Polygon62 | 116 | `$0.128k` | `$1.103` | 50.0% |
| local | not in Polygon62 | 13,574 | `$26.983k` | `$1.988` | 47.6% |
| yday | in Polygon62 | 1 | `$0.045k` | `$45.105` | 100.0% |
| yday | not in Polygon62 | 269 | `-$14.335k` | `-$53.290` | 49.1% |

This shows the broad PIT replay is genuinely a different book. The old 62-name yday edge does not
carry into the broader PIT universe; almost every broad-PIT yday trade is outside Polygon62.

Yearly yday behavior explains why the quality filters help but do not fully restore the old return:

| year | base B PnL | yday price >= 10 B PnL | yday vol20 <= 6% B PnL |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2018 | `-$3.325k` | `-$3.325k` | `-$3.325k` |
| 2019 | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` |
| 2020 | `$5.867k` | `$17.330k` | `$3.341k` |
| 2021 | `-$0.138k` | `$0.475k` | `$9.616k` |
| 2022 | `-$0.237k` | `-$1.470k` | `-$5.446k` |
| 2023 | `$3.303k` | `$7.832k` | `$8.558k` |
| 2024 | `$15.734k` | `$17.128k` | `$16.130k` |

The filter repairs 2020/2021/2023, but it worsens 2022. That makes it a real risk-rule candidate,
not a free lunch.

One more interactive probe dropped yday entirely from the broad PIT nowarmup run:

| portfolio | PnL | CAGR | DD | Sharpe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| B broad PIT base | `$29.361k` | 7.1% | `-$23.691k` | 0.271 |
| B broad PIT no yday | `$47.950k` | 10.5% | `-$36.379k` | 0.496 |
| B yday price >= 10 | `$46.127k` | 10.2% | `-$24.700k` | 0.416 |

Dropping yday improves PnL and Sharpe, but the drawdown becomes much worse. `yday price >= 10` is a
cleaner first repair than simply removing yday.

Conclusion:

- The low broad PIT return is mostly a universe/selection-bias finding, not a warmup artifact.
- Missing full-year 2016 remains a comparison caveat, but it is not the main explanation.
- Polygon62 yday was the hidden engine of the old lead (`$39.136k`), and that edge flips negative in
  broad PIT (`-$14.290k`).
- The next cheap work should be yday rule redesign / risk filters and ticker-fallback impact audit.
  Fetching 2016-2017 warmup is useful later, but it is not the fastest way to explain the low return.

### 6.132 Broad PIT yday redesign sweep

Question:

> If broad-PIT yday is the main reason return collapsed, can a simple yday risk rule restore the
> return profile without waiting for a long warmup fetch?

Script:

- `raits/research/stocks_pit_full_yday_redesign_variants_nowarmup.py`

- The script is resumable/incremental. It appends each completed `(variant, portfolio config)` row and
  skips completed rows if restarted.
- This run focused on the B portfolio and two reduced-yday-weight probes (`yday weight 0.10` and
  `0.20`) to keep runtime manageable.

- Do not promote these as final candidates. Treat them as hypotheses to pre-register and rerun in a

| ret60 <= -30% | 76 / 270 | `$82.273k` | 15.5% | `-$33.424k` | 0.596 | 0.904x |
| ret60 <= -20% and price >= 10 | 57 / 270 | `$94.406k` | 17.0% | `-$41.979k` | 0.681 | 0.888x |

The key discovery is `ret60 <= -20%`:

- The broad-PIT yday sleeve is not simply "bad stocks are bad." It is closer to a panic/crash-bounce
  effect that works after a severe 60-day selloff.
- The old yday rule on the broad universe failed because it also admitted overextended/event names.
- Keeping only `ret60 <= -20%` restores B CAGR to 17.2%, close to the Polygon62 lead's 17.8%, but
  drawdown is much worse (`-$35.372k` versus Polygon62 lead `-$14.216k`).

Risk trade-off:

| variant | interpretation |
|---|---|
| `ret60 <= -20%` | Best return repair, but drawdown still too high. |
| `ret60 <= -20% and price 10-100` | Highest Sharpe/PnL in this sweep, but DD `-$42k`; too aggressive. |
| `ret60 <= -20% and price 15-100` | Better balanced: CAGR 14.5%, Sharpe 0.635, DD `-$29.705k`. |
| `price 15-100` | Simple and less data-mined, but only CAGR 11.5%. |
| `vol20 <= 6%` | Best drawdown preservation, but weak return repair. |

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base, yday weight 0.10 | `$43.713k` | 9.7% | `-$30.369k` | 0.450 |
| base, yday weight 0.20 | `$38.520k` | 8.8% | `-$27.325k` | 0.384 |
| ret60 <= -20%, yday weight 0.20 | `$74.282k` | 14.4% | `-$36.019k` | 0.605 |
| ret60 <= -20% and price 15-100, yday weight 0.20 | `$62.829k` | 12.8% | `-$32.632k` | 0.584 |

Reducing yday weight does not solve the drawdown problem cleanly. It mostly reduces return while
leaving DD elevated.

Yearly B PnL for selected variants:

| year | base | price >= 10 | price 15-100 | ret60 <= -20% | ret60 <= -20%, price 15-100 | vol20 <= 6% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| 2019 | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` | `$8.157k` |
| 2020 | `$5.867k` | `$17.330k` | `$19.520k` | `$40.755k` | `$28.285k` | `$3.341k` |
| 2021 | `-$0.138k` | `$0.475k` | `$4.726k` | `$11.642k` | `$13.732k` | `$9.616k` |

Interpretation:

- Return collapse was fixable in-sample by changing yday from generic gapdown bounce into a severe
  selloff/panic bounce filter.
- 2022 remains the weak spot. The better yday filters improve 2020/2021/2023/2024 but do not solve
  the 2022 regime.
- The broad PIT candidate family is not dead, but it should stay WARN/research-only until the yday
  redesign is validated out of sample or at least with a pre-registered warmup-matched replay.

Next cheap checks:

1. Audit ticker fallback impact on these broad PIT variants.
2. Run a small pre-registered yday rule grid using only simple rules suggested here:
   - `ret60 <= -20%`;
   - `ret60 <= -20% and price 15-100`;
   - `price 15-100`.
3. Add 2016-2017 warmup later for final apples-to-apples comparison.

### 6.133 Broad PIT ticker-fallback impact audit

Question:

> Are the broad-PIT yday redesign results robust to rows where the PIT liquidity artifact had to use
> ticker-level fallback instead of cleaner security-id liquidity history?

Script:

- `raits/research/stocks_pit_full_ticker_fallback_impact_nowarmup.py`

Outputs:

- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_TICKER_FALLBACK_IMPACT_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_SUMMARY.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_TICKER_FALLBACK_IMPACT_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_YEARLY.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_TICKER_FALLBACK_IMPACT_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_SIGNAL_QA.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_TICKER_FALLBACK_IMPACT_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_TRADE_ATTRIBUTION.csv`
- `STOCKS_PIT_FULL_TICKER_FALLBACK_IMPACT_NOWARMUP_2026-09-13_YDAY_FALLBACK_TRADES.csv`

Important distinction:

- These are not mostly `pit_gate_mode` alias failures. The affected trades generally still match
  `exact_ticker`.
- The issue is `liquidity_metric_source == ticker_fallback`, meaning the PIT liquidity/prior-close
  artifact could not use the cleaner security-id path for that row and fell back to ticker-level
  history.

Signal fallback exposure:

| variant | sleeve | signals | ticker fallback signals | fallback pct |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| base | broad | 32,142 | 1,981 | 6.2% |
| base | local | 13,690 | 2,485 | 18.2% |
| base | yday | 270 | 63 | 23.3% |
| price 15-100 | yday | 134 | 28 | 20.9% |
| ret60 <= -20% | yday | 101 | 28 | 27.7% |
| ret60 <= -20%, price 15-100 | yday | 40 | 10 | 25.0% |

Actual rerun impact, B portfolio:

| variant | all rows PnL / DD / Sharpe | drop yday fallback | drop any fallback |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| base | `$29.361k` / `-$23.691k` / 0.271 | `$32.108k` / `-$31.005k` / 0.295 | `$29.900k` / `-$28.312k` / 0.283 |
| price 15-100 | `$54.052k` / `-$26.634k` / 0.485 | `$35.173k` / `-$23.265k` / 0.383 | `$33.630k` / `-$20.828k` / 0.378 |
| ret60 <= -20% | `$95.952k` / `-$35.372k` / 0.632 | `$73.331k` / `-$35.487k` / 0.559 | `$72.650k` / `-$31.592k` / 0.565 |
| ret60 <= -20%, price 15-100 | `$74.897k` / `-$29.705k` / 0.635 | `$51.118k` / `-$25.786k` / 0.523 | `$50.182k` / `-$24.761k` / 0.528 |

Trade attribution on `all_rows` shows why this matters:

| variant | yday non-fallback PnL | yday fallback PnL |
|---|---:|---:|
| base | `-$12.718k` | `-$1.572k` |
| price 15-100 | `-$8.950k` | `$13.134k` |
| ret60 <= -20% | `$18.105k` | `$13.627k` |
| ret60 <= -20%, price 15-100 | `$6.297k` | `$14.359k` |

The balanced redesign variant is especially exposed: `ret60 <= -20%, price 15-100` keeps only 40 yday
trades, and 10 ticker-fallback yday trades contribute `$14.359k` with a 100% win rate. That is too
fragile to treat as robust edge.

Examples of yday fallback winners in the redesign variants include `SERV`, `BTAI`, `QURE`, `NBR`,
`ARCT`, `VAPO`, `WVE`, `ESNT`, and `AMC`. Several rows have large adjusted/unadjusted-looking price
scale differences between trade entry prices and PIT prior-close fields, which is another reason to
keep this as a data-quality WARN rather than a promotion.

Conclusion:

- Ticker fallback is not fatal for the base broad PIT result, but it materially affects the attractive
  yday redesign variants.
- The headline in-sample yday redesign numbers should be haircut:
  - `ret60 <= -20%`: from `$95.952k` to about `$72.650k-$73.331k` when fallback rows are removed.
  - `ret60 <= -20%, price 15-100`: from `$74.897k` to about `$50.182k-$51.118k`.
- The fallback-stripped `ret60 <= -20%` result is still interesting: CAGR 14.2-14.3%, Sharpe
  0.56-ish, DD `-$31.6k` to `-$35.5k`. But it is no longer close to a production PASS.
- Before warmup fetch, the next cheap check should be a stricter identity/liquidity rebuild for these
  fallback names or a rule that explicitly excludes `liquidity_metric_source == ticker_fallback`.
